SPEAKING · STORY

Baz's first business

First, read the short Forward and warm up. Then study the 12 expressions and tell Baz's story in your own words.

Forward

Omsk, 1989. Foreign money can be dangerous. In the Soviet Union, people cannot freely buy and sell dollars. It is a serious crime. In 1961, two famous currency traders were finally sentenced to death. Foreign visitors are rare in many industrial cities, and some Soviet cities are closed to them. But a train from Beijing to Moscow stops in Omsk. It carries foreign passengers… and Baz has an idea. Will it bring him money — or trouble?

👋 Meet Baz

This is Baz. He is 16. He lives in Omsk in 1989. He has a business idea. He wants to earn money, help his family and be financially independent.

OPTIONAL · MORE CONTEXT

📚 Currency, fartsovka and Soviet restrictions

Why was foreign currency dangerous? Private buying and selling of foreign currency was illegal in the Soviet system. A famous 1961 case involved Yan Rokotov and Vladislav Faibishenko. They first received long prison sentences. The law was then made much harsher, the case was retried, and both men were sentenced to death and executed. The retroactive use of the harsher punishment became a notorious example of Khrushchev-era Soviet justice.

What was “fartsovka” (фарцовка)? It was illegal or semi-illegal trading in hard-to-get foreign goods — for example jeans, shoes, records and other Western products. Currency trading and fartsovka overlapped, but they were not exactly the same thing.

Why were foreigners special? Some Soviet towns and industrial areas had strict access rules. A number of cities were closed to foreigners because of military, scientific or industrial facilities. That is why an international train could be an unusual chance to meet foreign visitors.

Rokotov–Faibishenko case → 1964 International Commission of Jurists review (PDF) → Popular history: the 1961 currency case → What was fartsovka? → Fartsa TV series → Closed cities in the Soviet Union →

Teacher note: Baz’s comic is a classroom story. The links above give wider historical context; they do not mean that every detail of Baz’s story happened in the famous 1961 case.

READING + SPEAKING

Real job or fake job?

Read or listen. Click a picture if you want to see the full image. Choose Real/Fake for all six stories. Then use the one speaking recorder below to say which job seems the most real and which seems the most unreal.

🕵️ Job detective

Six teenagers have unusual jobs. Some stories are real. Some are fake. Read carefully and look for clues.

🔥 Warm-up

  1. What unusual jobs do you know?
  2. What can make a job story sound real: the task, the pay, or the place?
USA1

The Teen Tech Coach

High-school students in New Mexico can work for Teeniors. They already know a lot about phones and computers, so they help older people. They earn $15 an hour. The difficult part is explaining things slowly and patiently. One woman was surprised when a teen showed her an easy way to put photos on Facebook.

Denmark2

The Lost-Sock Detective

Sixteen-year-old Freja worked at a laundromat in Copenhagen. Many single socks were left there, so the owner asked her to photograph and match them. She earned 90 kroner an hour (≈ $14). Finding good pairs was difficult. One day she matched a banana sock with an avocado sock. People loved them and brought more single socks.

USA3

The Dog-Walking Friends

Matias, 13, and Bradley, 14, started walking dogs in Greenwich because they wanted local dogs to get more exercise. Their business got more customers, but finding new clients was difficult. In this classroom story, they earn $15 for one walk. One day a puppy ran after a squirrel. The boys finally found it sitting happily outside a bakery.

Japan4

The Queue Buddy

At 16, Haruto hated waiting in lines. A Tokyo company hired him as a Queue Buddy. Busy people paid him 1,200 yen an hour (≈ $7.30) to save their place. Waiting was boring. Once he waited five hours for a strawberry cake. The customer changed her mind and did not buy it, but she still paid Haruto.

South Africa5

The E-Bike Delivery Rider

At 19, Taylor Pitcher in Cape Town needed work to help her family. After training, she started delivering food by e-bike. Green Riders drivers average about R1,860 a week (≈ $112). The job can be dangerous. Taylor was once robbed at gunpoint, so now she often rides home with other delivery workers.

South Korea6

The Grandparent Gamer

At 17, Min-jun loved computer games and wanted an after-school job. A company in Seoul hired him to teach simple games to older people. He earned 12,000 won an hour (≈ $8.40). His challenge was teaching slowly and clearly. One 81-year-old woman practised for weeks and surprised her grandson by joining his online game.

GRAMMAR + PRONUNCIATION

Past Simple

1. Past Simple forms

🇷🇺 Как образуется Past Simple?
REGULAR · правильные глаголы
Обычно добавляем -ed: earn → earned, start → started.
Если глагол уже оканчивается на -e, добавляем только -d: exchange → exchanged.
IRREGULAR · неправильные глаголы
Общего правила нет — форму нужно запоминать: pay → paid, have → had, sell → sold.
Иногда форма не меняется: let → let.
💡 В вопросах и отрицаниях после did / didn’t используем начальную форму глагола: Did she get paid? · She didn’t leave school.

2. Complete the 100-word summary — learn the collocations

The completed summary has exactly 100 words. Choose the word that completes each useful phrase. Notice the words around every gap; this helps you remember the whole collocation.

Bree loves baking because she can be in the kitchen. She started cooking with her when she was five. At twelve, she told her mother she wanted to open a . Her mother suggested starting first. The business made enough , so they rented a shop. Bree goes to school, while her mother runs the store during the day. Running a business is challenging, but Bree learned to manage her time, work hard, be responsible and talk kindly to . Her cupcakes use fresh fruit and extracts, and people come back for more sweet treats every day.

SPEAKING · OPINION

Dream job — 1 minute

These four unusual jobs are real. Read or listen to the short A1/A2 descriptions, use the Russian hint if needed, then record your opinion.

NASA Curiosity Driver

You drive a rover on Mars from Earth. The rover has six wheels, cameras and a robot arm. Commands take time to reach Mars, so you must . People on the often study robotics, computer science or electrical .

Focus: What do you do? What skills do you need? Try: You need to be careful and good at technology.

Professional Criminal

Despite the funny name, this is a . A to try to break into a building, safe or computer system legally. You find weak points before real criminals do. You need security, IT or police and must explain how to make systems safer.

Focus: Who pays you? What problem do you solve? Try: The company pays you to find security problems.

Island Caretaker

You live on a tropical island, explore it, swim, take photos and write online about your experience. One famous spent six months near the Great Barrier Reef and over $100,000. The was huge, and island life could still be dangerous.

Focus: Where do you work? What do you create? Try: You work on an island and share your experience online.

Ice Cream Taster

You taste different ice creams and the flavour, texture and look. You do not simply eat ice cream all day. You need a good sense of taste and clear language to describe it. Many study .

Focus: What do you judge? What skills do you need? Try: You need a good sense of taste and clear language.
